    "text": "They mea\u0002sured everything and kept meticulous track of their\ndata—data that they generated through ongoing experi\u0002mental manipulation and variation. This hands-on\nexperimentation allowed them to collect data on how\ndifferent shapes and angles of attack affected lift. By sys\u0002tematically varying these parameters and observing the\noutcomes, they were effectively employing causal rea\u0002soning to identify the conditions under which lift could\nbe maximized. Their discovery and refinement of wing\nwarping for roll control was a direct outcome of under\u0002standing the causal relationship between wing shape,\nair pressure, and lift. Felin and Holweg: AI, Human Cognition, and Causal Reasoning\nStrategy Science, 2024, vol. 9, no. 4, pp. 346–371, © 2024 The Author(s) 359 The same processes of causal reasoning and directed\nexperimentation were also central for addressing the\nother two problems: propulsion and steering or control. And, more generally, the Wright brothers were careful\nscientists in every aspect of their attempt to realize their\nbelief in human-powered flight. For example, to deter\u0002mine a suitable place for their flight attempts, they con\u0002tacted the U.S. Weather Bureau. They had established\nwhat the optimal conditions might be for testing flight. They needed four things: consistent wind (direction and\nstrength), wide open spaces, soft or sandy landing sur\u0002faces, and privacy. They received several suggestions\nfrom the U.S.",

    "text": "- **Data-belief asymmetry.** Belief can legitimately exceed or contradict current data. Prevailing 1900s data said heavier-than-air flight fails. The Wrights held a contrary belief grounded in a causal theory, not in a sample.\n- **A theory is a bundle.** A problem framing, a causal mechanism, a contrarian hypothesis, and an experiment that could discriminate it. The Wrights reframed flight as a control problem, distrusted the published lift coefficients, built a wind tunnel, and generated their own lift tables.\n- **Intervention closes the loop.** The new data does not exist until the theory drives an intervention. Prediction from existing data can never produce it. This is Pearl's rung 2 and 3 against rung 1.",

    "document_title": "Theory Is All You Need — Felin and Holweg 2024 — complete published paper text",
    "text": "To offer a practical and vivid illustration of how\ndata–belief symmetry can be problematic, consider the\nbeliefs that were held about the plausibility of heavier\u0002than-air human-powered and controlled flight in the\nlate 1800s and early 1900s. (We introduce this example\nhere and revisit it throughout the remainder of the man\u0002uscript.) To form a belief about the possibility of human\u0002powered flight—or even to assign it a probability—we\nwould first want to look at the existing data and evi\u0002dence. So what was the evidence for the plausibility of\nhuman-powered flight at the time? The most obvious\ndata point at the time was that human-powered flight\nwas not a reality. This alone, of course, would not negate\nthe possibility. So one might want to look at all the data\nrelated to human flight attempts to assess its plausibility. Here we would find that humans have tried to build fly\u0002ing machines for centuries, and flight-related trials had,\nin fact, radically accelerated during the 19th century. All\nof these trials of flight could be seen as the data and evi\u0002dence we should use to update our beliefs about the\nimplausibility of flight. All of the evidence clearly sug\u0002gested that a belief in human-powered flight was delu\u0002sional. A delusion can readily be defined as having a\nbelief contrary to evidence and reality (Pinker 2021,\nScheffer et al. 2022): a belief that does not align with\naccepted facts.",
